newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr cautious as it waits on RBA.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr cautious as it waits on RBA.

text.p: A cautious Australian dollar spent the day avoiding testing either resistance and support as the market waited for Tuesday's quarterly report on the economy from the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA).
Trade was subdued with the U.S. market closed on Monday for a holiday, although early U.S. dollar strength in Asian trading benefited the Australian dollar on the cross rates.
By 4.30 p.m. (0530 GMT) the Australian dollar was at US$0.7639/44 from an early US$0.7642/47, having traded a US$0.7637-50 range on the day. It had closed local trade on Friday at US$0.7641/46.

"It is remarkably quiet given the volatility we had Thursday through Thursday night," Rob Hollonds, Dresdner Australian director of Treasury Services, said, referring to the unit's break of a two month downtrend resistance barrier.
Good support was expected from US$0.7630, which is above that downtrend line, but, at the same time, sellers were expected above US$0.7665 which capped the unit offshore.
Traders remained wary of Japanese security houses which had been big sellers in recent times, and who appeared on Friday to take the steam out of the dollar's resistance break.

With the U.S. closed, trade was seen remaining confined to narrow ranges ahead of the Tuesday's 3.00 p.m. (0200 GMT) release on Tuesday of the RBA's first detailed report on economic conditions since the December 11 rate cut.
Societe Generale chief economist John Edwards said he expected "the tone of the quarterly outlook to be cautiously optimistic on growth but threatening on wages growth."

The RBA is expected to echo made by Governor Ian Macfarlane last week that some effects of the three rate cuts last year were starting to appear, and that any decision on rates should wait for the outcome of the union movement's 'living wage' case.
"The bulletin should give us an indication of what the Reserve Bank's stance is on likelihood of another easing," Dresdner's Hollands said.
"If they're indicating between the lines that the economy has picked up, then you can write off an easing."
That would be supportive of the Australian dollar, with talk of a fourth rate cut one of the key factors undermining support since the last cut in December.
However, with the Japanese now favouring other high yielding currenices such as the U.S. dollar or sterling, analysts said it was unlikely to lead to a reversal of sentiment on the Aussie.

"The sentiment there in the second half of 1996 was that a continuation of dual currency samurais would see ongoing strength in the Australian dollar through 1997, and we've virtually seen a drying up of those dual currency samurais in 1997 to date, and that's really turned sentiment on the Aussie dollar around," SBC Warburg chief economist Peter Horn said.
Working against the dollar, was the fact that other high yielders were seen to be in, or near, tightening phases while the local outlook was not so certain.
On the crosses, the local dollar was a beneficiary of some early strength in the U.S. dollar, although trade was limited.
The local dollar closed off its highs, and down against the yen, after the U.S. dollar surrendered some early gains above 1.6960 marks and 124.60 yen.
At the close, the unit was at 94.97/07 yen and 1.2925/41 marks, from an early 94.94/04 and 1.2904/16 and a Friday close of 95.30/40 and 1.2890/04.

A three year high in the U.S. dollar against the Swiss franc saw the Australian dollar hit 1.1257 francs, its highest since May 1992. In trade weighted terms, it ended at 58.8 up a notch on Friday's 58.7.
